abstract: This paper presents the design and control strategies of the electronically controlled continuously variable transmission termed ECVT-II. ECVT-II has been developed by employing electronic control system for line pressure (belt clamping pressure) and pulley ratio, based on the current ECVT with a hydraulic control system. ECVT-II has obtained significant improvements in fuel economy and accelerating performance owing to the electronic control system. Further, driveability improvement in terms of smoothness while maintaining good response has been realized by applying the so-called 'fuzzy control" to the pulley ratio.

articleTitle: Antilock Braking System And Traction Control
abstract: It is exactly 10 years since we introduced an Antilock Braking System for passenger cars to the Automotive market. This system is commonly known as "ABS". After having got off slowly, by the mid-1980's, ABS gained more and more ground, first of all in Europe and then in the USA and Japan. Today, all over the world, countless drivers regard ABS as an important contribution to increasing safety on the roads. In the beginning of ABS development it was envisaged as a separate system (1)*, (2). That means, a system which could be combined without any trouble with the existing vehicle braking system. But soon after, the expectation came up that the integration of the ABS function within a hydraulic booster could result in cost savings. This was the reason why integrated ABS systems came on the market during the eighties, although we were forced in the process to realize that the integration of the functions meant that safety problems arose which could only be solved through considerable effort. In addition, hydraulic boosters are more expensive than vacuum boosters. Today, therefore, it has become obvious that integrated systems are limited to such applications where the higher costs are compensated by corresponding advantages. In the majority of applications, vacuum boosters with a separate ABS are used and for this reason I will deal with this version only.

articleTitle: The Next Step In Automotive Electronic Control
abstract: The salient feature of automotive electronics is not merely its ability to replace mechanical functions with electronic systems, but rather its flexibility in effectively joining individual mechanisms together. A wide variety of components employing electronic techniques have been developed and am presently being used in the automobile to meet divem marketplace requirements. A man-machine integrated control system is presented in this paper as the next step in automotive electronic control. In this connection, it is necessary to study ways of managing vehicle dynamics and human factors. In order to improve the relationship between the driver's perceptions and vehicle motion, a subjective control system with a human-like processor is expected to play a large role instead of the conventional objective one. New technologies, such as advanced control theory, artificial intelligence, fuzzy theory and neural networks wffl be employed in this human like processor.

The BMW 750 i, the top model in BMW's new 7 Series range, is powered by the first standard-production 12- cylinder engine to be made in Germany in about 50 years. This is the first automobile with interconnected electronic systems for controlling the engine, automatic transmission and driving stability. The paper describes the objective and concept of the drive train and driving stability electronics, the individual functions and their interplay. It also presents the various measures taken to make the drive management system absolutely reliable.

The following paper explains the various mobile and vehicle oriented communication systems and information principles serving the motorist in Western Europe. It comprises the fields of car radio with particular applications, cellular mobile radio telephones, country wide radio paging as well as location-finding and navigation including technical, political and market aspects of today and the medium range future.

articleTitle: Overview On Electronic Controls For Vehicular Diesel Engines
abstract: This paper clarifies the current and future technological subjects in terms of the societal and environment changes and technological improvements that concern diesel engines for commercial vehicles. The relation of these subjects and electronic technology, specific examples of electronics applications which have already been implemented and their influence on future technological concepts will be introduced.

Studies on productivity improvement in agriculture by automation of agricultural machines have been progressing rapidly in recent years. Some of them are already put into actual use, which are reported in this paper. They deal with automatic control of the working equipment of agricultural machines. The productivity of agricultural machines is expected to be improved tremendously when the technology of automatic vehicle guidance is put into practical use. As automatic guidance technology, an autonomous guidance system using simple input signals, an autonomous guidance system using input signals required for control extracted from multiple video information signals, and an externally assisted guidance system using a fixed laser oscillation source have been studied with respect to their properties. As a result, it has been found that selective use of these three systems according to the job requirements of agricultural machines will attain the above purpose.

articleTitle: European Concepts For Vehicle Safety, Communication And Guidance
abstract: Road traffic is an efficient and well accepted means of transportation and is still increasing in every country. What will it be like in the future? The European automotive manufacturers have initiated research work together with electronic and supplier companies, with traffic engineers and administrations towards an inte grated technical approach by using the foreseeable possibilities of electronics and infor- matics both in vehicles and for roadside equipment in order to increase traffic safety, environment compatibility and efficiency.

articleTitle: Automotive Electronics In The Car Of The Future: Strategic Alternatives For The Vehicle Manufacturer Motorola, Inc.'s Outlook For The Automotive Electronics Market
abstract: Automotive electronics is a rapidly growing market that is likely to contribute significantly to the vehicle's safety and performance. In this transition, automotive electronics is evolving from fairly simple, "hang-on" kinds of products to becoming one of the mainstream disciplines for building the car. This increasing complexity raises important issues for the vehicle manufacturer, including how to retain a span of control with a new and growing set of players in the business. The strategic choices facing the vehicle manu facturer take the question of automotive electronics beyond a mere technology issue to a strategic issue of participation and control

Parallel with progress in scientific technology, human capabilities have been expanded in combination with machinery. Concomitant with these marvelous advances, the styles of communications between machine and man are diversifying. The role of any man-machine interface is becoming more and more important with each advance in available technology. Take for example modern airplanes. Their performance and functions now extend far beyond the physical sensory and judgment capabilities of human beings. The man-machine interface in new aircraft must be reviewed and updated to correspond with rapid progress of the technology used in airplanes. In the past, a pilot had to have the capability to understand flying conditions at a glance from the information given by a number of gauges, and to make the correct judgment. Nevertheless, pilots were proud of this capability. The electronic display systems used in recent airplanes, however, permit pilots to selectively obtain the necessary information for each given instance and to make an informed decision. The introduction of electronic instruments has made increased maneuverability and safety for airplanes with a smaller flight crew possible In this paper, I will describe the current status, trends and the future of vehicle-use display systems which are desirable as man- machine interfaces, referring to products Nippondenso has developed and is currently producing.

articleTitle: Integrated Chassis And Suspension Controls Present And Future World Of Chassis Electronic Controls
abstract: Manufacturers of cars and trucks are becoming increasingly aware of the need to satisfy customer wants. In today's marketplace, customers demand the highest levels of quality and performance at affordable cost levels. The rapid evolu- tion of motor vehicles in recent years has resulted in a more knowledgeable and sophisticated customer body with much higher expectations. New motor vehicles are expected to pro- vide good ride and quiet operation as well as precise handling, steering and sure, confident braking. In times past, it was not possible to meet apparently conflicting chassis requirements with existing hardware. Good handling brought with it a firm ride and high effort steering. Smooth and quiet ride was often accompanied by poor directional stability and tendency to pitch and bounce over undulating surfaces. Modern vehicles are meeting these conflicting objectives through a marriage between chassis systems and electronic controls. The market for these chassis electronic control sys- tems is still developing, and not likely to reach maturity dur- ing the next decade. This paper addresses the present status and future direction of chassis electronic control systems. It speaks to present production systems and future directions. Program and technical management issues are covered next, concluding with some thoughts on the role of suppliers in this process.

Vehicles can now be located by satellite which means that a central control facility, such as a trucking company dispatch center, is able to know accurately the position of its trucks in near real time over a large geographical area. There are several methods of locating vehicles by satellite. The paper describes these methods, both existing and planned, and provides estimates of perfor- mance and cost.

articleTitle: Application Of Truck Electronics From The Viewpoint Of The System Integrator
abstract: This paper presents the performance,goals and rationale for integrating electronic systems into medium and heavy duty trucks. Successful integration of these systems with today's trucks requires careful planning and a thorough "top down" vehicle system design. Each sector of the design must be documented by way of component and subsystem specifications or drawings. These forms of documentation serve their purpose when they are reviewed often during the active design phase and interfacing components are verified for compatibility. Providing an electrical component that meets its own electrical and environmental specifications will not always insure that the component will function properly when installed in the vehicle. Further, details and examples are presented to demonstrate these points. It is very critical that the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and aftermarket suppliers should closely evaluate and analyze what effect a new electronic component may have on a vehicle's performance. Truck owners must realize that a modern vehicle is a collection of interacting systems and not merely a collection of parts.

articleTitle: Designing Automotive Electrical/electronic (E/E) Systems For Vehicle Assembly And Service
abstract: Increasing electronic feature content and electrical system complexity give rise to an ever growing challenge for vehicle assembly and service. Electrical/Electronic (E/E) system design contains some key elements for "building it right" and "servicing it right" - the first time. Thoughtful system planning and integration can provide an E/E execution which not only minimizes the proliferation of assembly and service processing steps, but also may actually eliminate some of these steps. An integrated E/E system has the capability of interacting and participating with vehicle assembly and service; the vehicle itself taking on some of the tools of production and test. Whereas the process requirements for assembly and service are often satisfied by the same design, accommodation of unique (and sometimes conflicting) requirements need to be reckoned with. This paper will attempt to provide an overview on how an integrated E/E system designed for assembly and service can help manage the automotive electronic explosion.

This paper presents an overview on the current state of the art of smart power semiconductors with a special emphasis on automotive applications. As an example the Siemens smart SIP- MOS technology is described and two families of standard devices especi ally suited for such applications are presented in detail. An outlook for smart power devices in the automotive environment from the perspective of a semiconductor manufacturer concludes this presentation

The need for better performance, safety, and comfort with reduced pollution of the environment is the driving force for the remarkable growth in automotive electronics. This growth has been and will continue to be directly related to improvements in the performance, cost, and reliability of microelectronics. This paper reviews the improvements that have been made in microelectronics since the invention of the integrated circuit in the late 1950s, delineates why the techniques that produced these improvements will have reached their limits in the near future, and proposes new technologies that will continue to increase microelectronic functionality per unit size and cost into the next century. Considered are the limits of scaling, three-dimensional circuits, artificial intelligence, design automation for circuit synthesis and first pass reliability, CMOS, bipolar, BiCMOS, gallium arsenide, gallium arsenide on silicon, biochips, quantum coupled devices, and cellular automata. Candidate markets that will be spawned by these technologies are discussed.

This paper surveys the evolution of the U.S. telecommunications system, including regulatory and technological events, which have dramatically altered the tra- ditional application of communication satellite systems. Satellites were originally intended to carry telephone traffic over "thick" routes and long distances. This applicaton, with a few exceptions, has now been taken over by fiber optic systems. However, satellites have several natural advantages over terrestrial technologies in applications that: Need broadcast (i.e., simultaneous point-to-multipoint) capability, Have low traffic volumes ("thin" routes) over long distances, or Require flexibility or mobility.

The increasing division of labor in commerce and industry is leading to a rise in the flow of goods. The resulting haulage capacity will still have to be provided mainly by trucks. The task, therefore, is to improve all the performance characteristics of trucks. Electronics will supply a significant contri bution. The trend will be towards the integration of subsystems which are still separate today. Information and communication systems will play avital role in the future exchange of data on board the vehicle and in improvements in freight transport organization. In conjunction with intelligent assistant systems supporting the driver, this will provide the conditions for realizing private traffic of the future in the form of an integrated system of cooperating partners.

This paper present a review of the history of automotive displays, the ergonomic aspects of modern driver information concepts, the state of the art of today's instruments, a comparison of various display techniques and, resulting from these considerations, the anticipated future trends for car displays in Europe.

For commercial vehicles engineering has concentrated in recent years on the development and introduction of electronically controlled systems. The paper reviews the present state, based on publications and discussions with vehicle manufacturers. Good agreement exists on the structuring of electronically controlled subsystems and on the objectives to be achieved with electronics. Only limited information is available on the strategies planned for introduction of electronics and approaches towards optimi- zation of the total vehicle. There is need for an early consensus on standards for a communication link between subsystems and for the future vehicle voltage supply system. Engine management will be the first electronically controlled subsystem used on a broader scale to meet emission standards.

The ever-increasing use of electronics and computers in our vehicles is apparent to everyone and many studies have clearly documented the dramatically increased electronic content in future vehicles. What's not so clear is how vehicle designers will take advantage of the increased possibilities represented by more electronics and computers to give the driver-vehicle system expanded capability and enhanced value to our customers. The essence of our work in Project Trilby is to create the concepts and bring together the technology for total, integrated control of our vehicles in order to provide our customers with a level of performance not otherwise achieveable. Total, integrated contro requires the coordination of all vehicle subsystems, while factoring the needs, performance and preferences of the driver into the design and control decisions. One possible scenario is an Adaptive Vehicle which would have: the capability for sensing or identifying its operational situation, an on-board knowledge or data base, the ability to analyze the situation relative to history and indicated driver preferences and performance capabilities, and then the ability to adapt the vehicle via control decisions to achieve the beat overall system performance. Worldwide, in the automotive industry and in other industries, there are similar efforts to capitalize on the continued maturing of computers and electronics, with the core question being the degree of intelligence and authority to be incorporated. The overall approach to design of such systems is dependent on: the use of analytical design techniques, including explicit representation of the driver, to understand configure the system; achieving coordinated control of the subsystems; and interfacing properly with the rapidly changing environment in which our vehicles must operate.

As in other industries, the application and impact of electronics have tremendously improved the function of automobiles. The application of electronic technology has provided higher performance, added convenience, more comfort, and greater safety for automobiles, in the areas of basic automotive functions, such as traveling, turning, and stopping, and in the other areas of display, convenience, entertainment and communication with society, etc. This report summarizes the current overview and future perspective in automotive electronics. Through the technologies of Toyota experimental vehicle, the FXV-II, this report enphasises that the keywords for the advanced technology in automotive electronics are "Integration', "Communication' and 'Intelligence".

The expansion of frequency allocation to the high-frequency ranges decided at WARC'79 has brought active development in millimeter-wave equipment. The development of new communication systems and new compound semiconductors have brought progress to the technology for high-frequency circuits and devices. We started the development of automotive radar using millimeter waves in the early 1970s, and have applied them experimentally for use in headway control. We are now studying new ways to use automotive radar taking into account the new technology in circuits and devices. This paper discusses the automotive radar we developed and outlines the problems that must be solved before practical use can be achieved.

articleTitle: Integrated micromachined silicon: vehicle sensors of the 1990's?
abstract: Intense global competition and the need to satisfy increasing customer demands for higher quality and better performance are driving vehicle manufacturers to accelerate the creation of more and better vehicle control These systems are affecting virtually all vehicle functions, including steering, sus- pension, and driver information, among others. Virtually all these systems use silicon-based electronics to store control algorithms, process information, and direct actuators to perform various functions. Although elec- tronics have been applied in many vehicles since the 1970's, the rapid growth period spanning the time-frame from 1985 to the end of the century has been commonly referred to as the automotive "electronics revolution". As this electronics revolution unfolds, however, sensor technology is not keeping pace. Sensor designs continue to be based on dated technologies, with inbred limitations, that could limit the capabilities of newer, more sophisticated automotive electronic control systems. Many electronics engineers and managers have identified "silicon" as the sensor technology which will close this technology gap and usher is even greater application of these control systems. This paper will examine both the current state of traditional sensor technology and "state-of-the-art" silicon technology. Reasons why silicon sensors hold great promise fo the future will also be addressed. Finally, predicitons on the growth potential of silicon sensors will be discussed as well as potential impediments to progress that could delay that growth.

articleTitle: Powertrain Sensors And Actuators: Driving Toward Optimized Vehicle Performance
abstract: During the next two decades, automobile manufacturers and automotive parts suppliers face the challenges associated with creating cost-effective improvements in sensor/actuator technology to increase vehicle reliability and quality in order to meet customer wants and needs. Focused upon powertrain sensors and actuators, this paper reflects upon the past, surveys the present, and offers a view of the future.

articleTitle: Trends Of Digital Signal Processing In Automotive
abstract: The advent of single-chip programmable digital signal processors (OSP) has expanded digital signal processing into automotive applications. Digital signal processors, compatible in cost to general-purpose microcomputers, offer much higher throughput in performing computationally intensive tasks. Because of this advantage, closed loop control, adaptive control, and digital audio processing can now be implemented in a cost effective manner. Some of the DSP automotive applications include combustion feedback engine control, active suspension systems, anti -skid brakes incorporating traction control and digital audio-based entertainment systems. The availability of digitaI signal processors i s changing many aspects of automotive designs. Early adopters of this technology for innovative automotive products wiII enjoy leadership and financial benefits over their competition. The impact of DSP to the automobile has just begun and will continue beyond the year 2000 ( I ) . This new technology has also presented tremendous challenges to both automotive and semiconductor industries. This paper first discusses digital signal processing characteristics. After reviewing historical digital signal processing solutions, the paper focuses on single-chip programmable digital signal processors and compares their architectural designs to general- purpose microprocessors and microcontrollers. Deficiencies of early digital signal processors are discussed and trends of DSP are explored. Performance and cost benefits of using DSP in digital control systems are explained. Automotive applications of digital signal processors are discussed in areas of powertrain, body and chassis control, and entertainment systems. The last part of the paper discusses the challenges presented to both automotive industry and semiconductor vendors.

articleTitle: The Systems Design Approach (better Late Than Not At All)
abstract: The Systems Design Approach, an emerging concept for the automotive industry, treats the total vehicle as one system vs. the vehicle as the result of a grouping of optimized components. It is a way of thinking that addresses very complex relationships and thus nurtures innovation. The systems process begins with a complete definition of the system requirements, is followed by the examination of technologies and generation of alternatives to satisfy those requirements, and concludes with the final development and proveout of the recommended alternative. The advantages of a Systems Design Approach are illustrated through an expla- nation of 6 types of system designs. There are inhibitors which result from the realities of the automotive industry and also drivers which help implement the concept. Implementing the Systems Design Approach will require now skills and affects not only product engineering, but also manufacturing and the supply base. It forces a re-thinking of ourtraditional concepts of dealing with quality. The thrust is that the automotive industry must maintain some component thinking, but the time is appropriate for increased utilization of the Systems Design Approach.

articleTitle: Electronic Control Of Car Chassis Present Status And Future Perspective
abstract: This paper discusses the present status, future trends and problems for development of electronic control technology of car chassis such as suspension, steering, braking and traction, and also describes the meaning and expected results of integrated control of each function.

articleTitle: Cummins Electronic Controls For Heavy Duty Diesel Engines
abstract: Cummins heavy duty diesel engines are being produced which have electronic control of their unit injection fueling systems. Engines with the PACE limited authority electronic control are on the road in some quantity while Cummins is also introducing the Electronically Controlled Injection (ECI) full authority system on its engines. The authors describe these engine controls and show how a "family of products" concept is resulting in a smooth introduction of this very different technology into the heavy duty diesel- powered industries. In particular, the Cummins family of products caters to the broad range of differences among end users in their familiarity with and readiness to accept electronics technology, by minimizing pos sible operating risks that otherwise might occur during the introductory transient.
